overview: Both are medical tools against infection, but a vaccine trains your immune system for the future while antiserum gives immediate, ready-made antibodies.
genZNote: Vaccine: teaching your body to fish. Antiserum: just handing your body the fish right now, urgently.

aspects.label: Mechanism
aspects.valueA: Contains a weakened/inactivated pathogen or its antigen, prompting the body to make its own antibodies (active immunity).
aspects.valueB: Contains ready-made antibodies against a specific pathogen or toxin, providing immediate protection (passive immunity).

aspects.label: Onset of Protection
aspects.valueA: Slower onset — takes days to weeks to build full immunity.
aspects.valueB: Immediate protection, since antibodies are already present.

aspects.label: Duration of Protection
aspects.valueA: Long-lasting, often for years, due to memory cell formation.
aspects.valueB: Short-lived, since no memory cells are formed by the recipient.

aspects.label: Typical Use Case
aspects.valueB: Emergency/therapeutic, given after exposure — e.g. rabies or snake antivenom.

overlay.examHighYieldNote: Antiserum provides immediate but temporary protection because it supplies antibodies directly, without triggering the recipient's own memory cell formation.
overlay.memoryTrick: Vaccine = train your immune system for later. Antiserum = urgent antibody delivery right now.
overlay.commonMisconception: Antiserum is not a substitute for vaccination — it offers no long-term memory response, so protection fades once the borrowed antibodies degrade.
